common_name: McDaniel's Cushion Moss Phlox (Vigorous Rose-Pink Creeping Phlox)

planting.note: Set out container divisions in early spring into lean, well-drained soil so roots knit in before summer heat arrives.

directions: Choose a sunny, sharply drained site, since McDaniel's Cushion rots quickly in soggy winter ground. This selection is noted for unusually vigorous, mounded growth and an exceptionally heavy flush of large, vivid rose-pink flowers that nearly hide the dark evergreen foliage each spring. Shear the mat back lightly right after flowering to keep growth dense and to encourage a tidy cushion rather than loose, sprawling stems. It tolerates poor, rocky soil far better than rich garden loam, making it a reliable choice for slopes, walls, and rock gardens.

common_name: Allegheny Smoke Moss Phlox (Lavender-Blue Creeping Phlox)

planting.note: Divide and transplant in early spring into gritty, fast-draining soil for the quickest mat establishment.

directions: Allegheny Smoke carries smoky lavender-blue flowers with a deep notch in each petal, giving the blooms a softer, more feathered look than the solid-pink moss phlox cultivars. Plant it where its cooler color can offset nearby hot pinks and reds, such as along a wall edge or rock garden border. It spreads into a tight, needle-leaved evergreen mat that smothers winter weeds and needs only an occasional post-bloom shearing to stay compact. Avoid heavy or constantly damp soils, which encourage crown rot in this species.

common_name: Betty Moss Phlox (Dwarf Purple Creeping Phlox)

planting.note: Plant small divisions in spring in a lean, gritty mix; this miniature selection is slower to bulk up than standard moss phlox.

directions: Betty is a true miniature selection of moss phlox, with foliage and purple flowers both scaled down from the typical cultivar, forming a tight button-like cushion rather than a sprawling mat. Its small size suits trough gardens, tufa rock plantings, and other confined rock-garden settings where a full-size moss phlox would overwhelm its neighbors. Give it the same lean, sharply drained conditions as other moss phlox, since excess moisture or rich soil causes it to rot or lose its compact habit. Because it grows so slowly, avoid crowding it with faster-spreading groundcovers.

common_name: Brittonii Rosea Moss Phlox (Fine-Leaved Pink Creeping Phlox)

planting.note: Install divisions in spring in lean, well-drained soil; this finer-textured selection is well suited to rocky or shale-like sites.

directions: Derived from the finer-textured Appalachian form of moss phlox, Brittonii Rosea forms a dense, low mat of especially slender needle-like leaves topped with pale pink spring flowers. Its compact habit and smaller foliage make it a good match for rock gardens, scree beds, and shallow-soil sites where the standard moss phlox cultivars can look coarse. It thrives in the same lean, gritty, well-drained conditions that suit its parent species and resents wet feet or rich soil. Light shearing after flowering keeps the mat tight and encourages fresh foliage through summer.

common_name: Ice Mountain Moss Phlox (Pastel Pink Creeping Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring in sharply drained, lean soil to help the mat establish before summer heat.

directions: Ice Mountain is a selection of the finer-leaved Appalachian form of moss phlox, bearing soft pastel-pink flowers over a dense, low mat of fine evergreen foliage. Its delicate color reads as paler and more muted than the brighter pink moss phlox cultivars, making it a gentle companion for white- or blue-flowered rock garden plants. Like other moss phlox, it needs full sun and lean, rocky, well-drained soil to stay compact and resist crown rot. A light post-bloom shearing keeps the carpet dense and promotes fresh growth for the rest of the season.

common_name: White Eye Moss Phlox (Pink with White-Eyed Creeping Phlox)

planting.note: Set out container divisions in spring into lean, well-drained soil so the mat fills in ahead of summer heat.

directions: White Eye covers itself each spring in medium-pink flowers, each marked at the center with a distinct ring of white that gives the overall planting a two-toned sparkle rather than a flat sheet of color. The needle-leaved evergreen foliage spreads into a tight, fast-filling mat that suppresses weeds and holds its color through a long bloom window. Grow it in full sun on lean to average, well-drained soil, since wet or heavy ground invites crown rot. Trim the mat back lightly after flowering to maintain a dense, cushion-like form.

common_name: Tiny Bugles Moss Phlox (Dwarf Near-White Creeping Phlox)

planting.note: Plant small divisions in spring in a lean, gritty mix, as this dwarf form bulks up slowly and dislikes being crowded.

directions: Tiny Bugles is one of a small group of miniature moss phlox selections with greatly reduced foliage and flower size, forming a very low, tight cushion of nearly white blooms in spring. Its diminutive scale makes it best suited to troughs, tufa, and small rock garden pockets rather than broad groundcover sweeps. It needs the same lean, sharply drained soil and full sun as larger moss phlox cultivars, but is slower growing and less tolerant of competition from vigorous neighbors. Keep it weed-free while it establishes, since its small stature makes it easy to overrun.
